final_task_tree.description: We're shipping a consumer mobile app that scans a user's face to verify identity at signup, and we charge a monthly subscription. Before launch I need to know, state by state, which biometric privacy laws apply to us, what notice and written consent we have to collect, how long we're allowed to retain the scan, whether there's a private right of action, and what the penalties are. Flag the states that are genuinely dangerous to launch in.

comments.body:
Starting. Scoping this as five research strands rather than 50 separate state lookups, because the law doesn't actually divide 50 ways — there's a small set of dedicated biometric statutes (IL, TX, WA, CO/CA amendments), a larger set of comprehensive consumer privacy laws that treat biometrics as sensitive data, and then a long tail of states with only breach-notification coverage.

Also flagging up front: your product has a second, separate exposure that isn't biometrics at all — the monthly subscription triggers auto-renewal / negative-option laws (FTC plus CA, NY and others). I'll cover that as its own subtask since "before launch" means both.

I am not a lawyer and this is not legal advice — this is a research memo to brief counsel with.

report.markdown:
# Biometric Compliance for a Face-Scan Identity App — 50-State Assessment

*Research memo to brief counsel with. Not legal advice.*

## The short version

Four things matter. Everything else is detail.

1. **Illinois will sue you; Texas will fine you.** These are the two genuinely dangerous states, for opposite reasons. Illinois has a private right of action and a plaintiffs' bar that has already extracted eight figures from companies doing *exactly what you are building*. Texas has an attorney general who took $1.4bn from Meta.
2. **Your product category has already been litigated.** Selfie-ID verification is not an untested edge case — Jumio and Onfido are the case law. You can read the complaints and pre-empt them.
3. **Don't build 50 versions and don't geofence Illinois.** One consent flow built to the Illinois standard over-satisfies every other state. The only real per-state variation you need is California's opt-out mechanics.
4. **The biggest lever is architectural, not legal.** If you discard the face template the moment the match returns, most retention exposure in every state disappears. Notice and consent obligations remain regardless — they attach at capture.

There is also a **second, unrelated exposure you didn't ask about**: the monthly subscription triggers auto-renewal law. Covered at the end.

---

## Are we even in scope? Yes.

Do not plan around an exemption.

| Regime | Definition | Us? |
|---|---|---|
| Illinois BIPA | "scan of face geometry" enumerated | **Yes** — settled by litigation against this exact product |
| Texas CUBI | "record of hand or face geometry"; no photo carve-out | **Yes** |
| Colorado § 6-1-1314 | biometric identifier, no volume threshold | **Yes, from user #1** |
| Comprehensive laws | biometric data processed *to uniquely identify* a person | **Yes** — that qualifier describes our signup flow exactly |

Two arguments might narrow scope; neither is safe to rely on:

- **Photograph exclusion.** Washington's RCW 19.375 expressly excludes photographs and video/audio recordings and data derived from them, and several Virginia-model laws do likewise. Useless in Illinois and Texas.
- **GLBA financial-institution exemption.** Argued in *Davis v. Jumio* — the vendor said its client was a financial institution — and it did not win a dismissal.

**Engineering point that catches people out:** deleting the raw photo does not take you out of scope. BIPA regulates "biometric information," meaning anything *based on* a biometric identifier used to identify someone. The derived template is covered after the source image is gone. **The retention clock runs on the template.**

---

## Tier 1 — Genuinely dangerous

### Illinois (BIPA, 740 ILCS 14)

The only state that combines a private right of action, statutory damages without proof of injury, a five-year limitations period, and a mature plaintiffs' bar.

**Four duties:**

| § | Duty |
|---|---|
| 15(a) | Public written retention/destruction policy. Destroy when purpose satisfied **or** 3 years after last interaction, **whichever first** |
| 15(b) | Before collection: written notice, specific purpose, specific length of term, signed written release |
| 15(c) | No selling, leasing, trading or otherwise profiting from biometrics |
| 15(d) | No third-party disclosure without separate consent |

**Damages:** $1,000 per negligent violation, $5,000 per intentional or reckless, or actual damages if greater, plus fees and costs. Under *Rosenbach v. Six Flags* (2019 IL 123186) a bare procedural violation makes a plaintiff "aggrieved" — no separate injury needed. That is why these cases survive motions to dismiss.

**The 2024 amendment helped, but only partly.** SB 2979 (PA 103-0769, effective Aug 2, 2024) overruled *Cothron v. White Castle*: repeated collections of the same identifier from the same person by the same method are now **one** recovery, not one per scan. The Seventh Circuit held in April 2026 that this applies retroactively to pending cases. It also confirmed **electronic signature counts as a written release**. Exposure is now roughly (class size × $1,000–$5,000) per violation *type* — capped, but for a consumer app still large.

**Precedent is directly on point:**

- ***Sosa v. Onfido***, No. 20-cv-04247 — ~**$28.5M** settlement over selfie ID verification, pleading both 15(a) (no public destruction policy) and 15(b) (no notice, purpose, retention term or release). Onfido was a *behind-the-scenes vendor*; users interacted with the client's app. That did not shield it.
- ***Davis v. Jumio Corp.***, No. 22 CV 776 (N.D. Ill. Feb 14, 2023) — motion to dismiss **denied**. Jumio separately settled an earlier matter for $7M.
- **Coinbase** — alleged sharing scans with Jumio and Onfido without separate 15(d) consent.

> Read across: whether you build the scanner or license it, **both you and your vendor are exposed**, and the pleading template already exists.

### Texas (CUBI, Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 503.001)

No private suits — AG-only — but the largest dollar risk in the country.

- **Duty:** inform before capture, obtain consent to capture. No published-policy requirement.
- **Retention:** destroy within a reasonable time and **no later than 1 year** after the commercial purpose expires.
- **Penalty:** up to **$25,000 per violation**.
- **The aggressive bit:** the Texas AG's litigating position is that unlawful collection *and* continued storage are **separate** violations — on that theory, one bad collection is up to **$50,000**. Meta settled for **$1.4bn**, described by the AG's office as the largest ever obtained by a single state.

Risk shape differs from Illinois: BIPA is many small claims aggregated; CUBI is one very large state action.

---

## Tier 1.5 — High, but less obvious

### Washington — the highest-variance state

Two overlapping laws:

- **RCW 19.375 (HB 1493)** — notice + consent (or an opt-out mechanism) before *enrolling* a biometric identifier for commercial purposes. AG-only, up to $7,500 per violation. Narrowed by the photograph exclusion.
- **RCW 19.373 (My Health My Data)** — this is the sharp one. **Broad private right of action** via the Consumer Protection Act, with plaintiff-friendly presumptions. Its "consumer health data" definition expressly enumerates biometric data, defined to include facial imagery from which a template can be extracted.

**Whether pure identity-verification biometrics are "consumer health data" is genuinely unsettled.** Our position would be that a scan carrying no health inference falls outside. Plausible, untested. This is the one question on the map where being wrong creates private-suit exposure outside Illinois. → subtask raised.

### Colorado — the sleeper

HB 24-1130, effective **July 1, 2025**, adding § 6-1-1314 to the Colorado Privacy Act: consent before collection; a **public** written policy covering retention, destruction **and breach response**; no sale/lease/trade; consumer right to access.

**It applies to any controller processing any amount of biometric data, regardless of the CPA's 100,000/25,000 thresholds.** Ten Colorado users and you are fully covered. Up to $20,000 per violation, AG and district attorneys, no private right of action.

---

## Tier 2 — Opt-in consent once you cross thresholds (~16 states)

Twenty states have comprehensive privacy laws in force in 2026. Biometric data is "sensitive data" in essentially all of them, requiring **opt-in consent** plus a data protection assessment, plus access/deletion rights on a ~45-day clock. **California is the exception** — opt-out / "limit the use of my sensitive personal information," not upfront opt-in.

CT · DE · IN · IA · KY · MD · MN · MT · NE · NH · NJ · OR · RI · TN · UT · VA (+ CA, CO, TX, WA covered above)

**Thresholds are the practical filter — and they are falling toward you.** Commonly 100,000 residents. But Rhode Island is 35,000, Maryland is 35,000, and **Connecticut drops from 100,000 to 35,000 in July 2026**. Treat thresholds as a timing question, not an exemption.

**Maryland (MODPA) is a product constraint, not paperwork.** Sensitive data may be processed only where **"strictly necessary to provide or maintain a specific product or service requested by the consumer,"** and it is the first state law to **prohibit the sale of sensitive data outright — consent cannot cure it**.

> Read-through: verifying identity at signup is very likely "strictly necessary." Training your matching model on user scans, contributing to a cross-customer fraud network, analytics, or marketing are likely **unlawful in Maryland no matter what the user agreed to**.

---

## Tier 3 — Baseline (~26 states)

No dedicated biometric statute, no comprehensive privacy law in force. Biometric identifiers appear only in **breach notification** statutes as protected personal information. No consent or retention duty; a breach involving templates triggers notification and, in several states, AG notice. Security controls plus an incident response plan covers these.

---

## Municipal

| Jurisdiction | Rule | Teeth | Reaches a mobile app? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **NYC** (Admin. Code §§ 22-1201–1205) | "Commercial establishments" must post signs near customer entrances; ban on selling/sharing/profiting from biometrics | **Private right of action** — $500 notice, $500 negligent, $5,000 intentional sale/share | Signage duty presupposes premises, so probably not — **but the no-profit prohibition is not obviously premises-limited** |
| **Portland, OR** (City Code Title 34, 34.10.010–.050) | **Outright ban** on private facial recognition in places of public accommodation | **Private right of action** — $1,000 **per day** | Probably not, but it's the only flat private-sector ban in the US |

Boston, San Francisco and Pittsburgh restrict government use only. Baltimore's private-sector provision has lapsed.

---

## The subscription problem you didn't ask about

Federal **click-to-cancel is dead**: the Eighth Circuit vacated the FTC's amended Negative Option Rule in its entirety in *Custom Communications, Inc. v. FTC*, No. 24-3137 (July 8, 2025), on procedural grounds, days before enforcement was to begin.

**This changes less than it sounds.** ROSCA, the original 1973 negative option rule, FTC Act § 5 and state UDAP laws all remain, and the FTC restarted rulemaking — a draft ANPRM went to OIRA on **January 30, 2026**.

**Build to California and you clear every state.** AB 2863 (signed Sept 24, 2024, amending Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17601–17602) requires: clear disclosure of price/frequency/cancellation before consent; **express affirmative consent to the renewal terms specifically**; proof of consent retained 3 years or 1 year post-termination, whichever is longer; an **annual renewal reminder**; advance notice of price changes; **cancellation in the same medium used to sign up**; no dark patterns. *Confirm exact operative dates with counsel — provisions phase in across 2025–26.*

> **Build note:** one consent-capture and audit-log system can serve both the biometric release and the auto-renewal consent. Both need durable, per-user, timestamped, versioned proof of what was shown and what was agreed. Don't build it twice.

---

## Recommendation

**Launch in all 50 states, on one compliance build, with the following non-negotiables.**

1. **Decide retention architecture first.** Ephemeral — match, return pass/fail, destroy template and image in-session, keep only a non-biometric audit record — removes most exposure everywhere and kills the 15(a)/CUBI destruction claims that were pleaded in *Onfido* and *Jumio*. If the product genuinely needs stored templates, the legal budget changes materially. **This decision gates the others.**
2. **One BIPA-grade consent screen, shown to everyone, in every state, before the camera activates.** Notice, specific purpose, specific retention term, separate affirmative release. Not in the ToS. Not bundled with the subscription consent. Separate named-vendor consent if an SDK transmits the scan.
3. **Publish the retention and destruction policy before the first scan.** *Mora v. J&M Plating* held the policy must exist by the time collection begins — publishing later does not cure the gap. Include breach response for Colorado.
4. **Never monetise, share, or train on the scans.** This single rule satisfies BIPA 15(c), CUBI's disclosure limits, Colorado, Maryland's absolute sale ban, and NYC's no-profit provision simultaneously.
5. **Get a written view on Washington MHMD** before launch. It is the only unsettled question that creates private-suit risk outside Illinois.

**Do not geofence Illinois.** Excluding your highest-risk state signals you knew the standard and chose not to meet it elsewhere — and the Illinois build is what you want everywhere anyway.

subtasks.title: Confirm whether a face scan for identity verification is a regulated "biometric identifier" under each statute type
subtasks.description:
THRESHOLD QUESTION: is our face scan a regulated biometric identifier? ANSWER: YES, in every regime that matters. Do not plan around an exemption.

- ILLINOIS BIPA: "scan of face geometry" is enumerated in the § 10 definition. Settled by litigation against this exact product category — selfie-ID verification vendors. Davis v. Jumio (N.D. Ill. 2023) denied dismissal; Sosa v. Onfido settled ~$28.5M.
- TEXAS CUBI: "record of hand or face geometry" is enumerated. No photograph carve-out.
- COLORADO § 6-1-1314: biometric identifier, no volume threshold.
- COMPREHENSIVE LAWS: sensitive data typically = biometric data processed FOR THE PURPOSE OF UNIQUELY IDENTIFYING an individual. That is a literal description of our signup flow, so the "unique identification" qualifier that narrows these definitions in other contexts does NOT help us — it targets us.

THE TWO ARGUMENTS THAT MIGHT NARROW SCOPE, AND WHY NOT TO RELY ON THEM:
1. Photograph exclusion. Washington RCW 19.375 expressly excludes photographs and video/audio recordings and data generated from them; several Virginia-model comprehensive laws similarly exclude physical or digital photographs. This could partially exclude us IF the pipeline is genuinely photo-only. It does NOT help in Illinois or Texas.
2. GLBA / financial institution exemption. Tried and failed to win dismissal in Davis v. Jumio, where the vendor argued its client (Binance) was a financial institution. Do not build a compliance plan on this.

CRITICAL ENGINEERING POINT — deleting the raw image does NOT take us out of scope. BIPA regulates "biometric information" defined as any information BASED ON a biometric identifier used to identify an individual. A derived face template/embedding is squarely covered even after the source image is destroyed. The retention clock runs on the TEMPLATE, not the photo.

ANSWER TO "HOW LONG CAN WE RETAIN IT": there is no single national number. Binding limits are — Illinois: purpose satisfied OR 3 years after last interaction, WHICHEVER IS FIRST. Texas: reasonable time, no later than 1 YEAR after the commercial purpose expires. Maryland: only while STRICTLY NECESSARY to the requested service. The intersection of those, for a scan used once at signup, is effectively "delete after the verification decision is made." See the recommendation in the report: match, return a pass/fail, discard the template.

subtasks.title: Research Illinois BIPA — consent, retention schedule, private right of action, damages
subtasks.description:
ILLINOIS BIPA — 740 ILCS 14. Highest-risk state in the country for this product. FINDINGS:

FOUR DUTIES (Section 15):
- 15(a): Must develop a WRITTEN, PUBLICLY AVAILABLE retention/destruction policy. Destruction deadline = when the initial purpose is satisfied OR 3 years after the individual's last interaction, WHICHEVER COMES FIRST. Mora v. J&M Plating (2022 IL App (2d) 210692) held the policy must exist at/before the time collection begins — you cannot write it later.
- 15(b): Before collection, must (i) give written notice that biometrics are being collected, (ii) state the specific purpose AND the length of term of collection/storage/use, and (iii) obtain a signed written release. Per the Aug 2024 amendment, electronic signature counts as a written release.
- 15(c): No selling/leasing/trading or otherwise profiting from biometric data.
- 15(d): No disclosure to third parties without separate consent. NOTE: if we use a third-party verification SDK, transmitting the scan to that vendor is a 15(d) event needing its own consent.

DAMAGES / PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION:
- Full private right of action, class actions are the norm. $1,000 liquidated per negligent violation, $5,000 per intentional/reckless, or actual damages if greater, plus attorneys' fees, costs and injunctive relief.
- Rosenbach v. Six Flags (2019 IL 123186): a bare procedural violation makes you "aggrieved" — no separate injury needed. This is why BIPA cases survive motions to dismiss.
- 5-year statute of limitations.
- Aug 2, 2024 amendment (SB 2979 / PA 103-0769) overruled Cothron v. White Castle: repeated collections of the same identifier from the same person by the same method = ONE recovery, not one per scan. 7th Circuit (April 2026) held this applies retroactively to pending cases. This materially caps exposure but does not remove it — with a consumer app, exposure is still (class size x $1,000-$5,000) per violation type.

DIRECTLY ON-POINT PRECEDENT — this exact product category has been sued repeatedly:
- Davis v. Jumio Corp., No. 22 CV 776 (N.D. Ill. Feb 14, 2023): selfie-ID facial verification vendor's motion to dismiss DENIED. Jumio also settled an earlier BIPA matter for $7M.
- Sosa v. Onfido, No. 20-cv-04247: ~$28.5M settlement over selfie ID verification, alleging both 15(a) (no public destruction policy) and 15(b) (no notice/purpose/retention disclosure/written release). Significantly, Onfido was a BEHIND-THE-SCENES vendor — users interacted with the customer's app, not Onfido — and that did not shield it.
- Coinbase litigation: allegations included sharing scans with Jumio/Onfido without separate 15(d) consent.

IMPLICATION: whether we build the scanner or license an SDK, both we and the vendor are exposed. Contractual flow-down and a joint consent screen are needed.

subtasks.title: Research Texas CUBI and Washington HB 1493 — the AG-enforced biometric statutes
subtasks.description:
TEXAS CUBI + WASHINGTON — both AG-enforced, no private right of action, but Texas is now the largest-dollar biometric risk in the country.

TEXAS — CUBI, Tex. Bus. & Com. Code § 503.001:
- Covers "a retina or iris scan, fingerprint, voiceprint, or record of hand or FACE GEOMETRY" captured for a commercial purpose. Our face scan is squarely in scope. Note there is NO photograph exclusion (unlike Washington).
- Duty: inform the individual BEFORE capture, and receive consent to capture. Texas does not require a published written policy the way BIPA 15(a) does.
- Retention: destroy within a reasonable time and no later than ONE YEAR after the commercial purpose for collection expires. § 503.001(c-1) extends this if another law mandates longer record retention. Indefinite retention with no deletion schedule is the single riskiest posture.
- No sale/lease/disclosure except within narrow statutory exceptions.
- Enforcement: TEXAS AG ONLY. Civil penalty up to $25,000 PER VIOLATION.
- WATCH THIS: the Texas AG's litigating position is that unlawful collection AND continued storage are SEPARATE violations — on that theory one non-compliant collection is up to $50,000. Meta settled with Texas for $1.4bn (2024), described by the AG's office as the largest ever obtained by a single state; Meta had earlier paid $550M in Illinois. The AG has made privacy enforcement a priority.
- Risk shape differs from Illinois: BIPA = many small claims via class action; CUBI = one very large state action.

WASHINGTON — two overlapping statutes:
1) RCW 19.375 (HB 1493, 2017). Prohibits ENROLLING a biometric identifier in a database for a commercial purpose without first giving notice, obtaining consent, OR providing a mechanism to prevent subsequent commercial use. AG-only enforcement via the Consumer Protection Act, penalties up to $7,500 per violation. IMPORTANT NARROWING: the definition expressly EXCLUDES photographs and video/audio recordings and data generated from them — depending on our pipeline this may put us partly outside 19.375. Do not rely on this without counsel.
2) RCW 19.373 My Health My Data Act — this is the sharper risk because it HAS a broad private right of action via the Consumer Protection Act. Its "consumer health data" definition expressly enumerates biometric data, defined to include facial imagery from which an identifier template can be extracted. Commentators describe the scope as far broader than the name suggests and compliance as extremely difficult. Whether pure identity-verification biometrics constitute "consumer health data" is genuinely unsettled — FLAG FOR COUNSEL, this is the main open legal question in Washington.

PRACTICAL: a BIPA-grade consent + retention program over-satisfies RCW 19.375 and CUBI. Build to Illinois and these two are largely covered, except for MHMD's separate privacy-policy and deletion-right mechanics.

subtasks.title: Map the comprehensive state privacy laws that classify biometrics as sensitive data requiring opt-in consent
subtasks.description:
COMPREHENSIVE STATE PRIVACY LAWS — 20 in effect as of 2026. Biometric data is "sensitive data" in essentially all of them.

THE 20 IN EFFECT (2026): California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Maryland, Minnesota, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oregon, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, Washington. Newest wave: Indiana, Kentucky and Rhode Island all took effect Jan 1, 2026.

THE COMMON RULE: sensitive data (which includes biometric data processed to uniquely identify a person) requires affirmative OPT-IN CONSENT before processing, plus a data protection assessment, plus access/deletion rights, usually with a 45-day response window. CALIFORNIA IS THE EXCEPTION — it uses an opt-out / "limit the use of my sensitive personal information" model rather than upfront opt-in.

APPLICABILITY THRESHOLDS ARE THE KEY PRACTICAL FILTER. Most of these laws only bite above a volume threshold (commonly 100,000 residents, or 25,000 if you derive >50% of revenue from selling data). So at low launch volume many of these do not yet apply. BUT:
- Thresholds are trending DOWN. Rhode Island is 35,000 (or 10,000 if >20% of revenue from data sales). Maryland is 35,000 / 10,000+20%. Connecticut DROPS from 100,000 to 35,000 in July 2026.
- COLORADO HAS NO THRESHOLD FOR BIOMETRICS AT ALL (see the HB 24-1130 subtask). Colorado applies from user #1.
=> Treat thresholds as a timing question, not an exemption. We will cross them.

MARYLAND (MODPA) IS THE STRICTEST AND NEEDS A PRODUCT DECISION:
- Sensitive data may only be collected/processed/shared where "STRICTLY NECESSARY to provide or maintain a specific product or service requested by the consumer." Consent does not cure it.
- MODPA is the first state law to PROHIBIT THE SALE OF SENSITIVE DATA OUTRIGHT, even with consumer consent.
- Read-through for us: using the face scan to verify identity at signup is very likely "strictly necessary." Using it for ANYTHING ELSE — training our matching model, contributing to a cross-customer fraud/identity network, analytics, marketing — is likely unlawful in Maryland regardless of what the user agreed to. This is a build constraint, not a paperwork constraint.

GLBA/HIPAA carve-outs exist in these laws (Maryland exempts certain GLBA financial institutions and HIPAA data). Do NOT assume we qualify — in Davis v. Jumio the vendor's argument that its client was a GLBA financial institution did not win it a dismissal.

subtasks.title: Identify the second-tier risk states — Colorado HB 24-1130, city ordinances, and breach-notification-only states
subtasks.description:
SECOND-TIER AND MUNICIPAL EXPOSURE.

COLORADO — HB 24-1130, effective JULY 1, 2025. This is the sleeper risk for an early-stage app.
- Adds § 6-1-1314 to the Colorado Privacy Act. Requires CONSENT before collecting a biometric identifier; a PUBLICLY AVAILABLE written policy covering retention, destruction AND breach response; prohibits sale/lease/trade of biometric identifiers; gives consumers a right to access their biometric data; extends to employees.
- CRITICAL: it applies to ANY controller processing ANY amount of biometric data, REGARDLESS of the CPA's normal 100,000 / 25,000 volume thresholds. A pre-launch startup with ten Colorado users is fully covered.
- Enforced by the Colorado AG and district attorneys under CPA § 6-1-112(1)(a). Civil penalties up to $20,000 per violation. NO private right of action.
- Substantively this is BIPA-shaped (consent + public retention/destruction policy + no sale), so a BIPA-grade build satisfies it.

MUNICIPAL — both are premises-based and PROBABLY do not reach a pure mobile app, but confirm with counsel:
- NYC Biometric Identifier Information Law (2021 NYC Local Law 3, NYC Admin. Code §§ 22-1201–22-1205, effective July 9, 2021). Requires a "commercial establishment" to post clear and conspicuous signs NEAR CUSTOMER ENTRANCES, and bans selling/leasing/trading/sharing or otherwise profiting from biometric identifier information. HAS A PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION: $500 per notice violation, $500 per negligent sale/share violation, $5,000 per intentional or reckless sale/share violation. The signage duty presupposes a physical location so it likely doesn't apply to us, BUT THE NO-PROFIT/NO-SALE PROHIBITION IS NOT OBVIOUSLY LIMITED TO PREMISES. Do not monetise the scans.
- Portland, OR (Portland City Code Title 34, ch. 34.10.010–34.10.050, effective Jan 1, 2021). Outright BAN on private entities using facial recognition in places of public accommodation within city limits. Private right of action, $1,000 PER DAY per violation. A remote mobile signup flow is likely outside "places of public accommodation," but this is the only US jurisdiction with a flat ban touching private actors, so get a written view before advertising in Portland.
- Baltimore's private-sector face recognition provision has lapsed/expired; Boston, San Francisco and Pittsburgh restrict GOVERNMENT use only and don't reach us.

REMAINING ~26 STATES: no dedicated biometric statute and no comprehensive privacy law in force. Biometric identifiers appear only in DATA BREACH NOTIFICATION statutes, which list them as protected personal information. Practical effect: no consent or retention duty, but a breach involving face templates triggers notification obligations and, in several states, AG notice. Baseline security + an incident response plan covers these.

subtasks.title: Research subscription auto-renewal law exposure (FTC negative option + CA/NY state laws)
subtasks.description:
SUBSCRIPTION / AUTO-RENEWAL EXPOSURE — separate from biometrics, same launch gate.

FEDERAL — the "Click-to-Cancel" rule is DEAD, but do not relax:
- On July 8, 2025 the Eighth Circuit, in Custom Communications, Inc. v. FTC, No. 24-3137, VACATED the FTC's amended Negative Option Rule IN ITS ENTIRETY, days before full enforcement was due to begin on July 14, 2025. Grounds were procedural — the FTC skipped a required preliminary regulatory analysis for a major rule under Magnuson-Moss.
- The rule would have required standalone consent to the negative-option feature (separate checkbox) and a simple click-to-cancel mechanism. Those specific federal requirements are gone.
- STILL FULLY IN FORCE: the Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act (ROSCA), the original 1973 negative option rule, FTC Act § 5, and state UDAP statutes. The FTC has continued enforcing under ROSCA.
- The FTC restarted rulemaking: on January 30, 2026 it sent a draft ANPRM on negative option practices to OIRA for review under EO 14215. A new rule is coming; build for it rather than against it.

CALIFORNIA IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT — build the flow to California and you clear every other state.
- AB 2863 (signed Sept 24, 2024) amends Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17601, 17602, hardening an already strict ARL. CONFIRM THE EXACT OPERATIVE DATE WITH COUNSEL — provisions phase in across 2025–2026.
- Requirements: clear and conspicuous disclosure of all terms (price, renewal frequency, cancellation method) BEFORE consent; "express affirmative consent" specifically to the automatic renewal terms; RETAIN PROOF OF EACH INDIVIDUAL'S CONSENT for 3 years, or 1 year after termination, whichever is longer; an ANNUAL RENEWAL REMINDER stating the service, the frequency and amount of charges, and how to cancel; advance notice of any fee change; cancellation must be available in the SAME MEDIUM the consumer used to sign up (i.e. if they subscribed in the app, they must be able to cancel in the app); express anti-dark-pattern rules.
- New York has a comparable ARL; most other ARL states are subsets of California's.

BUILD IMPLICATION: one consent-capture and audit-log system can serve BOTH the biometric consent record and the auto-renewal consent record. Design them together — both need durable, per-user, timestamped, versioned proof of what the user was shown and what they agreed to. Do not build these twice.

subtasks.title: Produce the state-by-state risk tier table and launch recommendation
subtasks.description:
SYNTHESIS — risk tiers. Full table in the report attached to the parent task.

TIER 1 — GENUINELY DANGEROUS. Do not launch without counsel sign-off.
- ILLINOIS. The only state combining a private right of action, statutory damages without proof of injury (Rosenbach), a 5-year limitations period, a mature plaintiffs' bar, and a track record of eight-figure settlements against selfie-ID verification vendors specifically. Even post-2024-amendment, class-wide exposure is (users x $1,000-$5,000) per violation type.
- TEXAS. No private suits, but the AG is the most aggressive biometric enforcer in the country: $1.4bn from Meta, up to $25,000 per violation, and a litigating position that collection and storage are separate violations (so up to $50,000 per user).

TIER 1.5 — HIGH, LESS OBVIOUS.
- WASHINGTON. RCW 19.375 is AG-only and has a photo carve-out, BUT My Health My Data (RCW 19.373) has a broad private right of action and expressly enumerates biometric data in its consumer health data definition. Unsettled whether ID-verification biometrics qualify. Highest-variance state on the map.
- COLORADO. No private right of action, but NO VOLUME THRESHOLD — binds us from user #1, unlike every other comprehensive law. Up to $20,000/violation, AG + district attorneys.

TIER 2 — OPT-IN CONSENT + DPA REQUIRED ONCE WE CROSS THRESHOLDS (~16 states).
CT, DE, IN, IA, KY, MD, MN, MT, NE, NH, NJ, OR, RI, TN, UT, VA. Biometrics are sensitive data requiring opt-in consent. Mostly dormant at low volume (typically 100k residents), but thresholds are falling — RI 35k, MD 35k, CT drops 100k -> 35k in July 2026.
- MARYLAND is the outlier within this tier and is a PRODUCT constraint, not a paperwork one: sensitive data only where STRICTLY NECESSARY to the requested service, and an absolute ban on selling sensitive data that consent cannot cure.
- CALIFORNIA sits here but operates on an opt-out / "limit the use of my sensitive personal information" model rather than opt-in.

TIER 3 — BASELINE (~26 states). No consent or retention duty; biometrics appear only in breach-notification statutes. Security controls + incident response plan suffices.

MUNICIPAL: NYC (private right of action, $500-$5,000, but premises/signage-based) and Portland OR (flat ban on private facial recognition in places of public accommodation, $1,000/day, private right of action). Both probably miss a pure mobile app; confirm.

THE CENTRAL CONCLUSION: do NOT build 50 compliance variants, and do NOT geofence Illinois. Build ONE flow to the Illinois standard and it over-satisfies every other state. The one genuine per-state variation needed is California's opt-out mechanics.

THE HIGHEST-LEVERAGE DECISION IS ARCHITECTURAL, NOT LEGAL: if the face template is discarded immediately after the match decision and never stored, most retention exposure across all tiers disappears, and BIPA 15(a)/CUBI destruction-deadline claims — which were pleaded in both Onfido and Jumio — largely evaporate. Notice and consent duties remain regardless, because they attach at CAPTURE.

subtasks.title: DECISION: choose the retention architecture — ephemeral template vs. stored template
subtasks.description:
This is the single highest-leverage decision and it belongs to you plus the eng lead, not to counsel. Options:
(A) EPHEMERAL — capture scan, generate template, match against ID document, return pass/fail, destroy template and image within the session. Retain only a non-biometric audit record (timestamp, result, consent version).
(B) STORED — keep the template to support re-authentication, duplicate-account detection, or a fraud network.

Why it matters: option A removes almost all retention exposure across every tier (BIPA 15(a), CUBI's 1-year clock, Maryland's 'strictly necessary' test) and kills the destruction-policy claims that were pleaded in Sosa v. Onfido and Davis v. Jumio. Option B keeps every one of those live and additionally makes Maryland and Colorado hard.
Notice and consent duties apply either way — they attach at capture.
If the product needs option B, say so now, because it changes the legal budget materially.

subtasks.title: Have counsel review the Washington My Health My Data question — does ID-verification biometric data count as 'consumer health data'?
subtasks.description:
The one genuinely unsettled legal question on the map, and the only one where getting it wrong exposes us to a private right of action outside Illinois.
MHMD (RCW 19.373) enumerates biometric data within 'consumer health data' and defines it to include facial imagery from which an identifier template can be extracted. It carries a broad private right of action via the Washington Consumer Protection Act, with plaintiff-friendly presumptions. Commentators have described perfect compliance as close to impossible.
Our position would be that a scan used purely for identity verification carries no health inference and falls outside the Act. That is plausible but untested.
Ask counsel for: a written view, and if the answer is 'arguably in scope', what the MHMD consumer health data privacy policy and deletion-right mechanics would require of us.

subtasks.title: Draft the BIPA-grade biometric consent screen and get it reviewed
subtasks.description:
One screen, shown to ALL users in every state before the camera activates — do not geofence, the Illinois build over-satisfies everywhere else.
Must contain, per 740 ILCS 14/15(b): (1) written notice that a biometric identifier is being collected, (2) the SPECIFIC PURPOSE, (3) the SPECIFIC LENGTH OF TERM for which it is collected, stored and used, (4) a separate affirmative action constituting a signed written release — electronic signature is expressly permitted since the Aug 2024 amendment.
Must NOT be buried in the general ToS or privacy policy, and must not be bundled with the subscription consent.
If a third-party verification SDK is used, add separate disclosure and consent for transmission to that named vendor — BIPA 15(d). The Coinbase litigation alleged exactly this failure.
Capture and durably store: user ID, timestamp, the exact text version shown, and the affirmative action taken.

subtasks.title: Write and publish the public biometric retention and destruction policy before any user is scanned
subtasks.description:
Required by BIPA 15(a) and by Colorado § 6-1-1314 (which also requires it to cover BREACH RESPONSE, not just retention and destruction).
Must be publicly available — a linked page on the marketing site and in-app, not buried in the privacy policy.
Must state a retention schedule and destruction guidelines meeting the strictest applicable clock: destroy when the initial purpose is satisfied OR within 3 years of the user's last interaction, whichever comes FIRST (Illinois), and no later than 1 year after the commercial purpose expires (Texas).
TIMING IS A LIABILITY IN ITSELF: Mora v. J&M Plating held the policy must exist by the time collection begins. Publishing it after launch does not cure the gap. This must go live BEFORE the first scan.

subtasks.title: Get the biometric vendor contract reviewed for BIPA flow-down and indemnity
subtasks.description:
Only applies if we license a third-party face-scan/liveness SDK rather than building in-house.
Both parties are exposed: in Sosa v. Onfido the vendor was purely behind the scenes — users interacted with the customer's app — and that did not shield it (~$28.5M settlement). Davis v. Jumio survived a motion to dismiss on the same facts. Expect the vendor to have been sued before and to know it.
Ask for: written BIPA/CUBI/CPA compliance warranties; a contractual commitment on the destruction schedule matching our published policy; confirmation the vendor does not use our users' scans to train its own models or to populate a cross-customer identity network (this would breach Maryland's sale/secondary-use limits and BIPA 15(c)'s no-profit rule); uncapped or separately-capped indemnity for biometric privacy claims; and audit rights.

subtasks.title: Build the subscription flow to the California ARL standard and log consent separately from biometric consent
subtasks.description:
Federal click-to-cancel is vacated (Custom Communications v. FTC, 8th Cir., July 8 2025) but ROSCA, FTC Act §5, state UDAP and state ARLs all still apply, and the FTC sent a new ANPRM to OIRA on Jan 30 2026.
Build to California (Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 17601-17602 as amended by AB 2863) and every other state is covered:
- clear and conspicuous disclosure of price, renewal frequency and cancellation method BEFORE consent
- express affirmative consent specifically to the auto-renewal terms, unbundled from the biometric consent and from the ToS
- retain proof of consent 3 years, or 1 year post-termination, whichever is longer
- annual renewal reminder: service, charge frequency and amount, how to cancel
- advance notice of any price change
- cancellation available in the SAME MEDIUM used to sign up (signed up in-app = must be cancellable in-app)
- no dark patterns
CONFIRM THE EXACT OPERATIVE DATE of the AB 2863 provisions with counsel; they phase in across 2025-26.

subtasks.title: Confirm with counsel whether NYC and Portland municipal rules reach a mobile-only app
subtasks.description:
Low probability, high consequence — both carry private rights of action, so a wrong call is expensive.
- NYC Admin. Code §§ 22-1201-22-1205: duties attach to a 'commercial establishment' and the notice duty is signage 'near customer entrances', which presupposes physical premises. But the ban on selling/leasing/trading/sharing or otherwise profiting from biometric identifier information is not obviously premises-limited. Damages $500 per notice violation, $500 negligent and $5,000 intentional/reckless for sale/sharing.
- Portland City Code Title 34, ch. 34.10.010-34.10.050: outright ban on private use of facial recognition in 'places of public accommodation' within city limits. $1,000 per day, private right of action. The only flat private-sector ban in the US.
Question for counsel: does a remote mobile signup by a resident inside those city boundaries create exposure, and does our data handling touch the NYC no-profit prohibition?

subtasks.title: Set a calendar review for falling privacy-law thresholds
subtasks.description:
We are currently below the applicability thresholds of most comprehensive state privacy laws, but that is a function of user count, not of law, and the thresholds are moving toward us.
Diary these:
- JULY 2026: Connecticut's threshold drops from 100,000 to 35,000 consumers.
- Already low: Rhode Island 35,000 (or 10,000 if >20% of revenue from data sales); Maryland 35,000 (or 10,000 + 20%).
- Colorado biometrics: NO threshold, applies now.
Action: set a recurring quarterly review that compares per-state active user counts against each threshold, with an owner. The failure mode is crossing a threshold silently and being non-compliant for a quarter before anyone notices.
